Attacks to Ukraine’s energy infrastructure have created an estimated $91 billion
in reconstruction needs. The World Bank Group is supporting the Government of
Ukraine to develop a European Union (EU)-aligned energy sector strategy to restore
security of supply, reestablish financial viability, mobilize private capital at scale,
strengthen corporate governance of state energy companies, and improve financial
sustainability — essential ingredients for economic competitiveness, productivity, and
employment creation.

The World Bank Group is also offering Ukraine comprehensive financial and technical
support. Re-PoWER, a World Bank trust fund-financed project, secured $403 million in
grants to restore electricity and heating for millions of people. In fiscal 2026, more than
$150 million of these grants were allocated for heating units, as well as for equipment
needed to secure power imports from the EU. Another project is rehabilitating
hydropower plants and delivering reliable power to affected communities.

In close coordination, IFC’s €50 million financing and support from partners unlocked
the private investment to build a new 189 megawatt (MW) wind power plant by the
Ukrainian company OKKO, complementing an earlier 147 MW project. The two projects
are expected to contribute to Ukraine’s energy grid stability and provide electricity to
around 800,000 people. Together with additional renewable energy projects supported by
IFC and partners, these private sector investments are expected to add approximately
715 MW of new capacity.

The World Bank Group is also promoting private sector resilience in Ukraine. IBRD is
supporting policy reforms across several economic sectors and helping to keep basic
services for firms and citizens, while IFC has established risk-sharing facilities with
Ukrainian financial institutions to support on-lending to micro, small, and medium
enterprises; mobilized private sector participation in infrastructure, including telecom
and energy; supported businesses to safeguard jobs and food security; and backed
innovation and high-tech ventures through venture capital and private equity funds
to retain talent and build future growth. For its part, MIGA has extended and increased
guarantees to free up capital linked to two banks’ mandatory reserves, issuing
$448 million in new guarantees since February 2022 to keep small businesses
afloat and maintain employment opportunities.

Brazil’s family farms employ nearly 10 million people and play a central
role in food production. Our partnership with the government, launched
in fiscal 2026, aims to support 1 million family farms with improved
technology, market logistics, and insurance by 2030.
This partnership is part of the World Bank Group’s strategic priority
that aims to move 300 million farmers from subsistence to surplus.
Our three-pillar strategy leverages the World Bank Group’s unique
capabilities. First, the World Bank and IFC strengthen the foundations
of family farms by investing in physical and human capital, such as rural
roads and research. Then, they align regulations, streamline standards,
repurpose subsidies, and remove barriers to doing business. Finally,
the World Bank Group expands access to finance through MIGA’s
guarantees and insurance, as well as partnerships created by the
World Bank and IFC. The private sector is a critical partner across
all three pillars.

With this approach, we’ll create an integrated pathway for family
farms to access markets, finance, technology, and resilience tools.
We’re working quickly because family farms around the world, including
500 million smallholder farmers, produce most of the world’s food,
yet many remain in poverty, relying on traditional farming methods
and lacking access to markets, finance, and technology. Supporting
them to become commercially successful is critical to creating jobs,
reducing poverty, and improving global food security. Our strategy
unlocks the knowledge, capital, and political will to seize that potential.

Pacific Island countries face some of the world’s highest rates of premature death and
disability from non-communicable disease, including diabetes, cardiovascular disease,
and cancer, alongside persistent communicable diseases. Local healthcare systems
struggle to provide care to dispersed populations, and the resulting inefficiencies drive
up service costs and hamper job creation and long-term growth.
The World Bank’s Pacific Healthy Islands Transformation (PHIT) project, approved in
fiscal 2026, is taking a new approach to improving the health of people across the
region. The $239.5 million project covers Fiji, Kiribati, Tonga, and Tuvalu, and — through
the Pacific Community — Naoero, Samoa, Solomon Islands, and Vanuatu.

Leveraging the expertise of Knowledge Bank teams at the World Bank and IFC, PHIT will
create, protect, and safeguard 16,000 vital health and health-support jobs across the
Pacific — spanning frontline service delivery, infrastructure development, digital health
systems, supply chains, and monitoring and evaluation — representing a major
investment in the region’s most critical asset: its people. AI-enabled diagnostics and
regional telehealth networks will enable more patients to receive accurate diagnostics;
expanded access to specialized services, including regional radiotherapy and advanced
medical imaging, will serve patients with specific needs. Together, these advancements
will accelerate regional health and development impact for greater resilience,
productivity, and inclusive growth.

PHIT is the largest World Bank Group multi-country operation in the Pacific and
supports our strategic priority of delivering quality, affordable health services to
1.5 billion people by 2030. It is also the first project developed with the Asian
Development Bank under the Full Mutual Reliance Framework, helping reduce
transaction costs. The OPEC Fund and the Pandemic Fund are also co-financing
PHIT, which is set to help Pacific Island countries establish the fundamental
conditions for good health, jobs, and growth.

Tourism is an engine of Cabo Verde’s economy, accounting for over a
quarter of GDP. But for years, the sector has been constrained by a narrow
model dominated by all-inclusive resorts in only two of the archipelago’s
10 islands, with few links to local businesses. Infrastructure deficits, a
shortage of skilled hospitality workers, and the absence of a coherent
framework for attracting quality investment left the country exposed and
its potential unrealized.
The World Bank Group has worked across its private and public sector
arms to help Cabo Verde chart a more diversified and inclusive tourism
sector. Two World Bank operations — the Resilient Tourism and Blue
Economy Development Project and the Improving Connectivity and Urban
Infrastructure Project — are strengthening the sector’s governance and
institutional framework, while upgrading critical infrastructure, including
coastal and jetty facilities, maritime passenger terminals, heritage sites,
and public spaces.

Two other programs — the Human Capital Development Project and the
Health Security Program in Western and Central Africa — are complementing
these efforts by strengthening essential services. Together they support
more than 100 vocational and specialty training courses, translating growth
into more and better-paid jobs.

IFC has anchored the private sector transformation. In December 2023,
IFC arranged a financing package of up to €35.5 million for Oásis Atlântico,
one of the country’s leading hospitality operators. The investment supports
more than 700 direct jobs and 20,000 indirect jobs, and linkages with over
700 small suppliers and farmers. IFC has also extended two successive
sustainability-linked loans to Cabo Verde Airports S.A., a subsidiary of VINCI
Airports, with the most recent reaching up to €60 million in February 2026.
The financing has modernized and greened the country’s seven airports,
created over 2,000 direct jobs and 1,200 indirect jobs, and helped establish
35 new air routes — driving a 60 percent surge in passenger volumes
since 2022.

The results are reshaping Cabo Verde’s tourism landscape. Average daily
tourist spending and overnight stays in previously under-visited islands
are both rising, and growing private investment signals confidence in the
country’s trajectory. With the World Bank Group supporting the full arc from
governance and infrastructure to skills and private finance, Cabo Verde is
building a more diversified, sustainable, and job-rich tourism economy.

India aspires to become an upper-middle-income economy in the next
decade. Its National Green Hydrogen Mission, which aims to catalyze
600,000 jobs by 2030, is critical to meeting this goal.
Since 2021, the World Bank Group has helped India advance
hydrogen hub planning, enabling infrastructure, and public-private
engagement to mobilize private sector investment. In fiscal 2026, IFC
invested $25 million in Hygenco Green Energies — its first direct green
hydrogen investment in India. This investment is complemented by
two IFC-managed blended finance facilities, the Clean Technology
Fund ($20 million) and the Frontier Opportunities Fund ($5 million),
which altogether enabled $55 million in co-investment from other
private sector partners.
The total financing package, including equity from other partners, will
support the creation of more than 1,000 direct and indirect jobs across
the green hydrogen value chain and broader industrial ecosystem over
the next five years.

This follows two previous financing commitments from the World
Bank, totaling $3 billion, to help India accelerate the development
of low-carbon energy. By promoting the development of a vibrant
market for green hydrogen, the World Bank Group is helping to create
jobs, strengthen India’s manufacturing base, and support long-term
economic growth.

BUSINESS OVERVIEW
PRIVATE CAPITAL MOBILIZATION

AND JOBS
The World Bank Group is adapting to meet the scale
of the jobs challenge, shifting from a provider of
finance to a platform that channels global capital
flows into developing countries. Rather than
relying principally on our balance sheets, we are
increasingly using financing, guarantees, data, and
our convening role to crowd private capital into the
most productive sectors for job creation. This means
building investable pipelines, creating mechanisms
that allow risk to be distributed across a broader
set of investors, and connecting a much larger pool
of global capital to development opportunities.
In fiscal 2026, we made real progress and changes that
are already translating into results. While financing
from the World Bank Group’s own resources rose from
$98 billion to $123.5 billion over the last five years,
private capital mobilization surged from $35 billion in
fiscal 2022 to $112 billion in fiscal 2026.

This more than
threefold increase represents a fundamental shift in
our ability to bring external capital into development
opportunities at scale, making us the largest mobilizer
of private capital among multilateral development
banks. Guarantees issued by the World Bank Group
Guarantee Platform grew by 46 percent in fiscal
2026. We are providing patient equity in markets
where early-stage capital is scarce and expanding
local-currency financing where foreign-exchange risk
would otherwise deter investment. We also began
piloting “originate-to-distribute” approaches to connect
institutional investors with emerging market assets at
greater scale. And we’re providing investors and ratings
agencies with historical data on the performance
of emerging market lending through the Global
Emerging Markets Risk Database. These practical
shifts are already supporting investment and jobs.
A NEW APPROACH TO

COUNTRY ENGAGEMENT
We are building a One World Bank Group client
coverage model that aligns public and private sector
solutions around jobs, growth, and private investment.
Our new approach is more efficient, outcome-focused,
and systematic in tapping private sector solutions
and will help countries tackle their development
challenges with greater speed, quality, and impact.
The centerpiece of this new approach is our
Country Partnership Framework (CPF) — the
key tool that guides our strategic engagement
with countries. CPFs typically span four to six
years, with a maximum duration of 10 years, to
align our support with a country’s development
goals and the World Bank Group Scorecard.

In fiscal 2026, we delivered 28 new CPFs that are
underpinned by five core diagnostics: Country
Climate and Development Reports, Country
Growth and Jobs Reports, Country Private Sector
Diagnostics, Poverty and Equity Assessments, and
Public Finance Reviews. From this data, we identify
three to five outcomes that support job creation,
and complementary public and private actions to
support the outcomes. With outcomes defined at the
intersection of three selectivity criteria — development
challenges, country development goals, and World
Bank Group comparative advantages — CPFs
serve as the primary vehicle for translating World
Bank Group targets and strategies into countrylevel action, delivering on client priorities through
complementary public and private solutions.

We also conducted our first cross-World Bank
Group business planning exercise in fiscal 2026.
We intend to make this an annual event so we can
better respond to government needs and adapt
our programs to evolving country contexts.

SUPPORT TO SMALL STATES
Small states4 face distinct challenges, including
remoteness, heavy import dependence, narrow
economic bases, and high exposure to external shocks.
The World Bank Group is expanding its resources to
help small states address these challenges. In fiscal
2026, IBRD/IDA portfolio net commitments to small
states reached $8.9 billion, IFC portfolio exposure
reached $682 million, and MIGA exposure reached
$790 million.
We are also intensifying our focus on climate
adaptation for small states. As of June 30, 2026,
30 small states have signed on to at least one
arrangement from the Crisis Preparedness and
Response Toolkit. In fiscal 2026, we published Country
Climate and Development Reports for Botswana,
Gabon, The Gambia, Mauritius, Namibia, and
Seychelles. We are preparing reports for seven more
small states — Barbados, Belize, Equatorial Guinea,
Fiji, São Tomé and Príncipe, Solomon Islands, and
Timor-Leste — to be published within the next two
fiscal years.

During the Spring Meetings in April 2026, the
World Bank Group launched the Small States
Strategy. Guided by select solutions underpinned
by the World Bank Group Jobs Framework, the Strategy
prioritizes interventions with the greatest potential
to support job creation and economic growth.
Support will be differentiated to reflect individual
country contexts, while using regional approaches,
aggregated procurement, capacity building, and
stronger partnerships to address scale constraints,
high transaction costs, and partner fragmentation.
Implementation is anchored in Country Partnership
Frameworks. The Strategy was informed by feedback
from small states gathered through consultations
and engagement, including at the annual Small States
Forum held alongside the World Bank Group Annual
Meetings in October 2025.
For more information, visit https://www.
worldbank.org/en/country/smallstates.
SUSTAINABLE FINANCE

IN CAPITAL MARKETS
IBRD has mobilized finance for middle-income
countries for more than 75 years, raising over
$1 trillion from capital markets since issuing its first
bond in 1947. In fiscal 2026, IBRD, which is rated
triple-A by the major credit rating agencies, raised
nearly $50 billion through Sustainable Development
Bonds issued in a variety of structures and maturities.
Please see the IBRD’s annual Impact Report for more
information about how funds raised in the capital
markets support IBRD-financed projects.
IDA also issues Sustainable Development Bonds
to scale up its development impact, and in fiscal
2026, issued approximately $14 billion in bonds.
Read IDA’s Impact Report to learn more. In March
2026, following action by the United States (U.S.)
Congress, securities issued or guaranteed by IDA
joined IBRD and IFC as “exempted securities” by the
U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.

IFC’s green and social bonds are an integral part of its
borrowing strategy with $2 billion and $4 billion issued
in fiscal 2026, respectively. In January 2026, IFC issued
a three-year $2 billion social bond with proceeds
funding a diverse range of social projects which include
affordable basic infrastructure (e.g., clean drinking
water, energy, transport); access to essential services;
food security and affordable housing; and womenowned small- and medium-sized businesses, among
other sectors. Read more in IFC’s Green and Social Bond
Annual Impact Report.
FINANCIAL INNOVATIONS TO

MAXIMIZE DEVELOPMENT IMPACT
Shareholder support for IBRD’s innovative financing
instruments continued to grow in fiscal 2026,
strengthening our capacity to scale lending and tackle
global challenges. Singapore pledged funds to our
hybrid capital instrument and New Zealand became
the first shareholder to subscribe to our Enhanced
Callable Capital instrument, bringing hybrid capital
contributions to $1.2 billion. Together, these new
instruments demonstrate IBRD’s strong leveraging
power, turning $1 into $6-10 of additional lending over
time, and unlocking tens of billions for global impact.
IBRD has continued to structure outcome bonds that mobilize private capital for
specific development projects. For example, in December 2025, IBRD issued a
$200 million principal-protected bond, the Clean Cooking Outcome Bond, that
mobilized private capital to support the distribution and use of cleaner cooking
stoves in Ghana.

This outcome bond provides investors with a coupon that includes
a fixed guaranteed component, and a variable component linked to the sale of carbon
credits generated from the use of the cookstoves. This is the first outcome bond
linking investors’ financial return to the generation of Internationally Transferred
Mitigation Outcomes, with the governments of Ghana and Switzerland authorizing
the cleaner cooking projects supported by this bond.
In April 2026, IBRD priced a $120 million principal-protected Spekboom Restoration
Outcome Bond to support large-scale ecosystem restoration and job creation in South
Africa’s Eastern Cape province. The 14-year bond offers investors a return linked to
the successful restoration of spekboom, a native plant with high carbon sequestration
capacity. Under the structure, $25 million is provided as up-front financing for
the project, which aims to restore about 50,000 hectares of land and to create an
estimated 11,000 local jobs.

THE STEP-UP LOAN
Designed to increase IBRD’s impact,
the Step-up Loan (SuL) addresses
the infrastructure gap in developing
countries. Loan costs are lower during
the project phase, letting assets reach
full capacity. Clients can refinance
with private capital once projects are
proven viable. During refinancing, we
provide technical assistance and credit
enhancement through MIGA or IFC.
This approach accelerates IBRD’s capital
recycling and boosts lending capacity
over the long term. Indonesia’s stateowned utility used the SuL for a second
time in fiscal 2026, bringing its total
commitment to $1.1 billion across two
energy projects. The Indian state of
Rajasthan also secured $215 million for a
transport project to enhance road safety
and growth.

DELIVERING MORE FOR CLIENTS
Further promoting private capital mobilization, we
helped countries refinance their outstanding IBRD
loans on now-proven projects where lending can be
considered “de-risked” from a commercial lender’s
perspective. For India, this approach unlocked nearly
$1.5 billion in new borrowing capacity from IBRD.
We advanced the Framework for Financial Incentives,
which offers volume, tenor, and price incentives, to
encourage clients to undertake projects that address
global challenges with cross-border benefits. Under
the framework, Tunisia became the first country
benefiting from a 43-year IBRD loan, eight years
more than the current 35 years, and received
$150 million beyond the country allocation by
signing a $430 million financing package to
support energy sector modernization.

IFC’s local currency and structured finance instruments
are central to its mission of channeling private
capital to businesses and communities that need
it most. Guarantee and risk-sharing platforms
help financial institutions expand credit to small
businesses, the backbone of employment in
developing countries, with transactions in Georgia,
Guatemala, India, and Mexico expected to generate
up to 22,400 direct and indirect jobs from IFC’s
investment in Banco G&T Continental alone.

approach unlocks private investment and delivers
results at scale by leveraging each institution’s unique
strengths while working cohesively toward shared
development objectives.

AND FINANCIAL MODEL
IBRD finances its loans through its own equity and by
borrowing in the capital markets via the issuance of
IBRD bonds to fund development projects in member

Standard & Poor’s, and investors view its bonds as highquality and liquid securities. IBRD’s funding approach
continues to aim to achieve the best long-term value
for borrowing members on a sustainable basis. IBRD’s
ability to channel the funds it raises in international
capital markets to developing member countries is
important in achieving its goals.
IBRD’s approach has enabled it to borrow at favorable
market terms and pass the savings on to its borrowing
members. Funds not immediately deployed for lending
are held in IBRD’s investment portfolio to provide
liquidity for its operations. In fiscal 2026, IBRD raised
nearly $50 billion by issuing medium- and long-term
bonds in a variety of currencies.

As a cooperative institution, IBRD does not seek to
maximize profit but rather to earn enough income to
ensure the long-term financial capacity necessary to
sustain its development activities. Allocable net income
in fiscal 2026 was $2.3 billion, and out of this, the
Executive Directors approved the allocation of
$1.1 billion to the General Reserve, and recommended
to the Board of Governors an allocation of $750 million
to IDA and $500 million to Surplus. Further, the Board
recommended to IBRD’s Board of Governors the
following transfers out of Surplus: $300 million to the
IBRD Trust Fund for Gaza and West Bank, $100 million
to the Grant Facility for Project Preparation, and
$100 million to the IBRD Surplus-Funded Livable Planet
Fund. As part of its lending, borrowing, and investment
activities, IBRD is exposed to market, counterparty,
country credit, and operational risks.

The World Bank Group’s Chief Risk Officer (CRO)
leads the risk oversight function covering financial,
operational, model, and environmental and social
risks. The CRO also supports the institutional decisionmaking process through dedicated risk committees
that cover financial, operational, and franchise risks.
In addition, IBRD has implemented a strong risk
management framework to support management in
its oversight functions. The framework is designed to
enable and support IBRD in achieving its goals in a
financially sustainable manner. One summary measure
of IBRD’s risk profile is equity-to-loans ratio, which
is closely managed in line with its financial and risk
outlook. As of June 30, 2026, this ratio was 21.6 percent,
and IBRD’s cumulative subscribed capital totaled
$332.5 billion, including $23.6 billion in paid-in capital.

BUILDING NEW AND IMPROVED PLATFORMS

FOR MOBILIZING PRIVATE CAPITAL
Large institutional investors, such as pension funds,
insurance companies, and asset managers, typically
allocate capital through standardized asset classes
and systematic distribution rather than for individual
transactions. IFC’s originate-to-distribute business
model is designed to meet those needs by creating
diversified packages of assets — across multiple
projects and markets — that are structured in a
form that is recognizable and can be in some cases
independently rated. The originate-to-distribute
pathway includes existing mobilization products with
significant investor engagement, such as B loans, while
broadening IFC’s approach to investor participation
through more systematic and standardized channels of
distribution, including securitization.

In September 2025, IFC launched the Emerging Markets
Securitization Program (EMSP), a significant step
forward in our originate-to-distribute program. EMSP
recycles IFC’s loans into packaged securities in which
investors such as asset managers, pension funds, and
insurance companies can invest. The $510 million
transaction was listed on the London Stock Exchange,
giving visibility, pricing transparency, liquidity, and
the prospect of secondary trading. The second
transaction under the EMSP was completed in June
2026, demonstrating its ability to replicate and scale.
These transactions benefited from a catalytic equity
co-investment from the UK Government’s Mobilist
Program alongside IFC.

IFC further expanded its originate-to-distribute
program in fiscal 2026 with the inaugural Trade Finance
Synthetic Securitization (TFSS). The TFSS is composed
of $500 million trade assets originated under IFC’s
Global Trade Finance Program, which has more than
half its portfolio in low-income and fragile and conflictaffected states. The transaction’s private capital
mobilization ratio is up to 1:19, meaning for every
dollar of risk retained by IFC, up to $19 are taken
up by private investors.
The originate-to-distribute model that underpins
the EMSP and TFSS can be standardized and scaled,
providing an efficient means to draw substantially
more private capital into emerging markets.

IFC also continued to build upon proven platforms for
mobilizing private capital at scale. One of the most
effective is the Managed Co-Lending Portfolio Program
(MCPP), a portfolio syndications platform through
which investors can gain exposure to a diverse mix of
loans to private sector borrowers in emerging markets.
In fiscal 2026, the MCPP mobilized $6 billion from 19
global insurers to support lending to financial
institutions in emerging markets. By sharing the credit
risk on a portion of IFC’s loan portfolio, the program
frees up balance sheet capacity and is expected to
support up to $10 billion in new IFC financing to
small- and medium-sized enterprises. It is IFC’s largest
mobilization under a single agreement.
ADDRESSING THE SHORTAGE OF EQUITY

IN EMERGING MARKET FIRMS
Equity is the scarcest form of financing in emerging
markets and the foundation for sustainable business
growth. IFC is working to increase its own equity
investments while developing new ways to bring equity
from other investors into developing economies.
IFC has expanded its capacity to deploy junior equity
by investing $100 million of its net income to seed
the Frontier Opportunities Fund. The fund allows IFC
to take on more complex risk positions and crowd
in private capital, including senior equity, to unlock
investments in the most challenging markets. Eight
projects have been Board-approved. As of June 30,
2026, an additional $100 million has been allocated
to the Frontier Opportunities Fund, allowing IFC to
meet the burgeoning pipeline of projects. The portfolio
covers a wide range of sectors, including carbon
finance, energy access and transition, green hydrogen,
and industrial transformation.

EXTENDING MORE CAPITAL AND
SUPPORT TO MSMEs
Reaching micro-, small-, and medium-sized enterprises
is central to the jobs challenge. These businesses are
the largest employers in developing economies, yet
they are often the hardest to serve. IFC is expanding
its reach through digital platforms, supply chain
integration, and tailored financing — going beyond
financial institutions to connect entrepreneurs more
directly to capital and markets.

Integrating into supply chains can propel growth for
smaller enterprises. To that end, a new risk-sharing
facility launched in fiscal 2026 with Standard Chartered
is designed to strengthen supply chains for businesses
across Africa. The partnership introduces supply
chain finance solutions in eight markets: Côte d’Ivoire,
Egypt, Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa, Tanzania,
and Zambia. Over the next three years, it is projected
to enable about $1.9 billion in supply chain finance
transactions, supporting more than 500 suppliers in
both domestic and global value chains.

CREATING MARKETS IN FRAGILE AND
CONFLICT-AFFECTED COUNTRIES
Fragile, conflict-affected, and violence-affected
(FCV) countries are where the private sector gap is
widest and the need for jobs most urgent. By 2030,
nearly 60 percent of the world’s extreme poor will

The International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID) supports cross-border
investment by offering an independent, specialized forum for the resolution of disputes. Effective,
impartial dispute resolution strengthens confidence among investors and States and enhances
predictability — core pillars of a favorable investment landscape.
ICSID is a unique institution, created by the Convention
on the Settlement of Investment Disputes between
States and Nationals of Other States. This multilateral
agreement, also known as the ICSID Convention, was
formulated in 1965 by the Executive Directors of the
World Bank.
ICSID is essential to the World Bank Group’s work to
accelerate job creation at scale, a strategy focused on
investing in the physical and human infrastructure
that people and businesses need to thrive, supporting
business-enabling environments, and mobilizing
private capital.

By providing an effective, impartial forum for resolving
international investment disputes, ICSID mitigates
perceived risk and encourages the mobilization of
private capital across borders. The availability of ICSID
to investors and States fosters trust and predictability,
helping create investment environments that drive
economic growth and job creation.

At the core of this work are ICSID’s dispute
administration services, which cover a range of
procedures including arbitration, conciliation,
mediation, and fact-finding for disputes arising from
investment contracts, international treaties, and
domestic investment laws. ICSID’s rules and procedures
are widely regarded as the gold standard for
investment dispute settlement, offering a stable and
predictable legal framework that balances the interests
of both States and investors and has been modernized
over time to reflect best practices in the field.
ICSID also supports the development of international
investment law and dispute settlement by producing
and sharing knowledge, building capacity, and
engaging with Member States and other stakeholders
on investment dispute prevention, management,
and settlement.

Fiscal 2026 saw meaningful progress across all these
areas, as ICSID advanced its priorities to deepen
engagement and knowledge, expand mediation and
amicable settlement, and uphold the highest standards
in case management.

up to $375 million. IFC is also acting as an accredited entity for a $220 million
concessional senior loan and a $75 million investment grant from the Green
Climate Fund. For its part, MIGA received Board approval for guarantees of
up to $1.25 billion.

Complementing the Aqaba-Amman project is IBRD’s $300 million Jordan
Water Sector Efficiency Project, which includes financing from partners. This
is strengthening Jordan’s broader water sector through non-revenue water
reduction, energy efficiency, and distribution-system readiness.
The World Bank Group’s support for Jordan’s water sector aligns with our
Water Strategy Implementation Plan, which outlines how investments,
long-term policy reforms, and institutional sustainability can deliver water
security, economic growth, and job creation.
